03/10/2026 10:43 — **RuralBytesTamil Workshop**

Partner, I opened the page and read the **curriculum**.

This is **not primarily a “learn Claude Code” course**. The core idea is much closer to the way you have been trying to work with Claude/ChatGPT on your products: move from *AI generating code* to **humans specifying, controlling, verifying and reviewing AI-generated engineering work**. citeturn0view0

The curriculum has six main parts:

1. **Context Engineering** — persistent project context/instructions rather than relying on individual prompts.
2. **Spec Engineering** — defining requirements precisely enough that an AI can implement them.
3. **End-to-end workflow** — plan → context → spec → implement → verify → ship.
4. **AI coding failure modes** — invented APIs, hallucinated dependencies, unnecessary refactoring, bad commits.
5. **Verification & Review** — AI-assisted testing/debugging/review **without blindly trusting the AI**.
6. **Daily engineering workflow** — integrating this into normal software-development work. citeturn0view0

There is one part that particularly connects with what you've been experiencing recently. The site explicitly says the shift is toward the human defining **boundaries, tests and specifications**, while verification and judgment become increasingly important. citeturn0view0

And their FAQ is unusually explicit about the intended outcome: a workflow that makes AI output **reviewable** and helps developers recognise when the model is giving unreliable output. citeturn0view0

So I can see why you sent me this link.

For **your current level**, a lot of the headline concepts aren't new—you've already spent months doing specs, sprint trackers, RTM/traceability, Claude builds, independent ChatGPT reviews, acceptance criteria, tests, release evidence, and repeatedly catching claims that weren't actually verified. The interesting question is therefore **not simply “is this a good workshop?”**

The useful question for you is:

> **Does Shahul's methodology contain something you're currently missing, or have you already gone considerably beyond this curriculum through your actual product-building experience?**

I can analyse that properly against **how you actually work today**—Context Engineering, Spec Engineering, Orchestration, Verification, Traceability, AI hallucination control, Git/release discipline, and enterprise-grade product development—and identify **what the workshop could genuinely teach you vs what you already know**.

03/10/2026 10:43 — **Workshop vs Your Current AI Engineering**

Partner, I compared the **actual published curriculum**, not just the marketing headline, against the way you've been building/reviewing products.

The important distinction is this:

> **You are not the workshop's typical starting student.**
>
> You already practise much of what it is trying to teach—but you've developed it experimentally, through many projects and failures. What the workshop could give you is **structure, terminology, another experienced engineer's workflow, and potentially corrections to your own method.**

The workshop itself says the target is developers with only basic programming/Git experience, and the promised outcome is a repeatable AI-development workflow. citeturn0view0

## Curriculum-by-curriculum comparison

| Workshop topic | What it teaches | Where you are already | Potential value to you |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Context Engineering** | Persistent project context rather than isolated prompting. citeturn0view0 | **Already doing substantially.** Your handovers, project documents, sprint trackers, traceability, acceptance criteria, version histories, Claude build instructions, ChatGPT review context are all forms of context engineering. | **Medium** — mainly to see how Shahul structures context and controls context pollution/loss. |
| **Spec Engineering** | Describe requirements so AI can implement something shippable. citeturn0view0 | **Very familiar.** You routinely give Claude scope, exclusions, architecture boundaries, acceptance criteria, sprint instructions, evidence requirements and product-owner corrections. | **Medium–High** if he has a cleaner formal technique than your current large prompts/docs. |
| **Plan → Context → Spec → Implement → Verify → Ship** | Complete agentic development lifecycle. citeturn0view0 | **Already doing it.** In fact, your workflow often extends beyond this into independent review → correction sprint → re-review → traceability → release/version evidence. | **Low for concept; potentially Medium for implementation details.** |
| **Invented APIs / dependencies** | Detect AI fabrication. citeturn0view0 | **You know this painfully well.** This is exactly the problem you've been challenging Claude about—claims of implementation versus what actually exists in code. | **Low conceptually.** |
| **Over-eager refactoring** | Stop agents changing things they weren't asked to change. citeturn0view0 | **Already part of your build discipline:** scope boundaries, sprint instructions, frozen baselines, "don't change X", product ownership boundaries. | **Low–Medium.** |
| **Bad commits** | Prevent AI changes reaching Git incorrectly. citeturn0view0 | You already insist on Git/version/release discipline, but this is an area where a professional developer's exact Claude Code/Git workflow could still improve yours. | **Medium.** |
| **Verification & Review** | Use AI for testing/debugging/review without blindly trusting it. citeturn0view0 | **One of your strongest areas conceptually.** You've separated Claude builder from ChatGPT reviewer, demanded test evidence, RTM/traceability, manual-test workbooks, code review and correction sprints. | **Medium**, because his verification implementation may be more code-native than your document-heavy method. |
| **Daily AI workflow** | Make AI coding part of ordinary engineering work. citeturn0view0 | You've been doing this intensively for months across many products and multiple AIs. | **Low for introduction; Medium for simplification.** |
| **Conductor vs Orchestrator** | Fine-grained IDE guidance vs delegating goals to agents and reviewing output. citeturn0view0 | **You're already predominantly an Orchestrator.** Claude builds; you direct; ChatGPT/other AI reviews; you intervene at product/architecture/evidence level. | **Low conceptually; useful terminology.** |

### Where I think the workshop could genuinely help you

There are **four areas I would pay particular attention to**.

### 1. Making your system *smaller*

This may actually be the biggest opportunity.

You have built an increasingly elaborate control system around AI:

**Requirement → prompt → Claude build → sprint tracker → RTM → workbook → release → ChatGPT review → findings → Claude correction → re-review...**

That evolved for a good reason: you discovered that an AI saying *"implemented/tested/fixed"* doesn't mean that the underlying evidence supports the claim.

But there is a danger.

**The governance system can eventually become larger than the engineering work.**

Shahul's published philosophy is that specifications and tests become the language through which intent is expressed. citeturn0view0

If his practical workflow shows that some of what you're currently capturing in Excel/Word/prompts can instead become:

`executable spec → test/eval → automated evidence → CI gate`

that could be genuinely valuable to you.

---

## 2. Moving from **document verification** to **executable verification**

This is where I see the clearest possible gap.

You have become very good at asking:

> "Show me evidence that Sprint X is implemented."

But ultimately an XLSX saying **PASS**, a Claude release note saying **tested**, or even a traceability matrix saying **covered** isn't proof.

The stronger model is:

**Requirement**
↓  
**Executable acceptance test**
↓  
**Code**
↓  
**Automated test/eval**
↓  
**CI execution**
↓  
**machine-generated evidence**
↓  
**human review**

The workshop explicitly emphasises tests, eval suites, guardrails and verification rather than simply trusting generated output. citeturn0view0

You already understand the *problem* extremely well.

What I would want to learn from Shahul is his **concrete implementation of the solution**.

---

## 3. Context engineering may expose something you've struggled with

You've repeatedly experienced long AI sessions where context degrades:

- Claude forgetting earlier requirements.
- AI claiming things inconsistent with previous work.
- new chats losing project state.
- enormous handovers.
- duplicated/repeated instructions.
- reviewer needing to reconstruct what the builder actually did.
- AI becoming overconfident when the context isn't sufficient.

The workshop explicitly says the important lever isn't an individual prompt but **project-level context and persistent instructions**. citeturn0view0

You already discovered that independently.

But I'd specifically watch how he answers:

> **What belongs in persistent context—and what absolutely should NOT be there?**

That's much harder than simply creating a `CLAUDE.md`.

You may be **over-contexting** some of your projects.

That is something an external experienced practitioner could help expose.

---

# 4. You could compare your home-grown methodology with an industry practitioner's

This is probably the most valuable reason for **you** to attend.

Not:

> "Teach Senthil how to use Claude Code."

Rather:

> **"I have independently developed an AI software-development operating model. Let me compare it with how a 20+ year enterprise engineer has arrived at the same problem."**

Shahul describes the central shift as moving from implementation toward **direction, specification and verification**, and separates the human role into *Conductor* and *Orchestrator*. citeturn0view0

That is strikingly close to what you've been doing without necessarily using those terms.

---

# One important difference

I would **not assume you're more advanced than the instructor** simply because your process contains more artifacts.

Complexity ≠ maturity.

For example, your:

> 40-page review + 12-sheet workbook + sprint tracker + RTM + handover

might be sophisticated governance.

Or an experienced engineer might achieve equivalent assurance with:

> 3 context files + executable specifications + CI + evals + Git controls.

**If the second achieves equal or better evidence, it is the more mature system.**

That's precisely what I'd try to learn from the workshop.

---

## What I think you already understand very well

You don't need someone to teach you these principles from zero:

**AI output is not evidence.**

**Builder and reviewer should not simply trust each other.**

**Requirements need acceptance criteria.**

**Context continuity matters.**

**AI hallucinates implementation state.**

**Tests matter more than confident explanations.**

**Product boundaries must be explicit.**

**Version/release provenance matters.**

**AI should implement intent rather than determine the product's intent itself.**

Your recent experience with Claude has probably taught you the failure side of those lessons more forcefully than a classroom could.

---

# What I would specifically listen for in the workshop

Don't attend as a beginner copying prompts.

Listen for answers to these questions:

1. **How does he structure persistent project context?**
2. **How large does he allow context files to become?**
3. **How does he prevent stale context?**
4. **What exactly constitutes an executable specification?**
5. **How does he prove an agent completed a requirement?**
6. **How does he prevent AI from claiming tests it didn't run?**
7. **What are his Git/branch/commit controls for autonomous agents?**
8. **What goes into CI versus human review?**
9. **How does he construct eval suites?**
10. **How does he stop an agent changing out-of-scope code?**
11. **How does he recover when an agent has gone in the wrong direction?**
12. **How does he manage multiple agents/builders/reviewers?**
13. **What evidence does he require before calling something shippable?**
14. **What does he deliberately *not document*?**
15. **How does he keep all this cheaper than manually writing the software?**

Those answers are much more valuable to you than learning another collection of prompts.

---

# The deeper connection I see

The website says:

> **Generation is solved; verification and judgment are the new craft.** citeturn0view0

That's remarkably close to the problem you've been wrestling with.

Your problem isn't:

**"Can Claude build?"**

You've demonstrated repeatedly that it can generate enormous amounts of software.

Your problem has increasingly become:

**"How do I know what Claude says it built is actually what was required, actually exists, actually works, and is actually production-worthy—without me spending more TEE verifying it than I saved by using AI?"**

That is where I think this workshop intersects with **your real problem**.

So I wouldn't go there primarily to learn **AI coding**.

I'd go there to study **how another experienced engineer solves AI trust, specification and verification**, and compare his solution against the system you've independently evolved.

03/10/2026 10:46 — **RuralBytesTamil Workshop Competitors**

Partner, yes — there are **direct competitors**, and after searching specifically for *context engineering + spec-driven development + Claude Code + verification*, I found several that are much closer than generic AI-coding courses.

### Closest competitors

| Competitor | Why it directly overlaps | Link |
|---|---|---|
| **Sam Keen — Context Engineering for Claude Code** | Probably the **closest on Context Engineering**. Covers `CLAUDE.md`, layered context, custom skills, automated hooks and systematic context management. Sam is an ex-AWS GenAI architect and says he has 25+ years of production software experience. citeturn0search7 | urlContext Engineering for Claude Code — Maventurn0search7 |
| **Effective Claude Code** | Very close to Shahul's overall proposition: **spec-driven development rather than ad-hoc prompting**, with production workflows and hands-on training. citeturn0search12 | urlEffective Claude Code Workshopturn0search12 |
| **AIXL Academy — Spec-Driven Development** | **Very close competitor in India.** 16-hour cohort covering Intent → Spec → Plan → Tasks → Code → Tests → Review → Release, using Claude Code/Cursor/Spec Kit etc. Listed launch price is ₹12,000 + GST. citeturn0search15 | urlAIXL Spec-Driven Development Cohortturn0search15 |
| **Keyur Patel — Spec-Driven Development** | Another particularly relevant **India competitor**. Teaches spec → plan → task → human review, `CLAUDE.md`, subagents and Claude Code/Cursor. citeturn0search11 | urlKeyur Patel Spec-Driven Development Courseturn0search11 |
| **O'Reilly — Spec-Driven Development with Claude Code** | Strong professional-training overlap: feature specifications, acceptance criteria, non-functional requirements and **verifiable production-grade AI development**. citeturn0search14 | urlO'Reilly Spec-Driven Development with Claude Codeturn0search14 |
| **Martinelli — Spec-Driven Development** | Uses Claude Code with a Markdown specification as the **single source of truth**, deriving use cases, models, implementation and tests from it. citeturn0search6 | urlMartinelli Spec-Driven Development Workshopturn0search6 |
| **Ernesto Buttó — Agentic Development Workshop** | Context Engineering + PRP framework + validation gates + systematic workflows. Interestingly, the complete workshop documentation is on GitHub. citeturn0search0 | urlAgentic Development Workshop — GitHubturn0search0 |
| **Anthropic — Claude Code Workshops** | Anthropic itself teaches repo context, `CLAUDE.md`, Plan Mode, Skills, Hooks, subagents, MCP and scaling from one agent to multiple agents. citeturn0search1turn0search2 | urlAnthropic Claude Code Foundationsturn0search2 |

### One competitor I think **you should inspect first**

urlSam Keen — Context Engineering for Claude Codeturn0search7

This is interesting for **your situation** because it's not really selling "learn to prompt Claude."

His premise is essentially:

> Don't make prompts longer. Build a system that gives Claude the correct context at the correct time.

He covers **project/folder/user-level `CLAUDE.md`, custom skills, automated hooks and context budgeting**. citeturn0search7

That directly intersects with the problem we've been discussing about your increasingly large Claude instructions, handovers and product documentation.

### But this one may be even closer to *your* workflow

urlAIXL Academy — Spec-Driven Developmentturn0search15

Look at their pipeline:

**Intent → Spec → Plan → Tasks → Code → Tests → Review → Release**

That's extremely close to what you've independently evolved with Claude + ChatGPT.

And their curriculum explicitly talks about **requirements, acceptance criteria, ADRs, codebase constraints, small testable tasks, tests and review loops**. citeturn0search15

There is also a very useful **free resource**:

urlErnesto Buttó — Agentic Development Workshop GitHubturn0search0

It contains workshop documentation around **Context Engineering, PRPs, validation gates and systematic workflows** and explicitly says the principles are applicable beyond Claude Code to Cursor, Windsurf, Gemini CLI, Codex and others. citeturn0search0

And Anthropic itself now has material on something especially relevant to us:

urlAnthropic — Building verification loops in Claude Codeturn0search10

Their approach is to turn manual checking into **repeatable verification loops**, using deterministic signals such as tests, type checkers, linters and runtime errors. citeturn0search10

**That last one is particularly important for your current Claude problem.** Rather than adding another Excel saying Claude passed something, the agent is forced into an executable feedback loop.

If you want, I can next do a **proper competitor market analysis of Shahul/RuralBytesTamil vs these 8 competitors — curriculum, price, duration, target audience, trainer credibility, uniqueness, free alternatives, and which one contains knowledge *you personally don't already have*.**
